description: Hi everyone! I'm a Science student with a strong interest in science, technology, and learning new things. I'm a curious and creative person who enjoys exploring ideas, solving problems, and working with people who share the same passion. I have good communication and teamwork skills, and I'm willing to learn, share ideas, and contribute to making our project successful. I'm particularly interested in projects that combine science and creativity to solve real-world problems.
summary: SpaceLegacy is an interactive 3D museum of NASA machines that were left on the Moon and Mars. It is made for students aged 10 to 16, families and classrooms. Visitors choose a world on a NASA map and meet four machines: Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage, its laser retroreflector, the Spirit rover and the InSight lander. They can rotate real NASA 3D models, tap numbered parts and learn what each part did and why it was built that way. Each machine then tells its own story in a short creative voice. The story is clearly labelled as creative, and every fact links to a NASA source. After the story, students try a small science activity, like timing a laser pulse to the Moon with t = 2d/c, and answer three questions. Most young people only hear about active missions. SpaceLegacy shows that these "abandoned" machines still have stories to tell, and that one of them still does science today.
details: What it does SpaceLegacy is a website that works like a small museum. It tells the story of four NASA machines that are still on the Moon and Mars: - Eagle's descent stage (Apollo 11, 1969): the lower half of the lunar module, which became the launch pad that sent Armstrong and Aldrin home. - The Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector: 100 glass corner cubes that observatories still use to measure the distance to the Moon. - The Spirit rover (2004 to 2010): built for 90 Martian days, it worked for about six years and found signs of ancient hot springs. - The InSight lander (2018 to 2022): it listened to Mars shake and recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes. How it works Each visit follows one simple path: choose a world, find a machine, look at it in 3D, read its story, try an activity and answer a few questions. - Moon and Mars maps: markers sit at the published landing sites on NASA global maps. - 3D viewer: students can rotate and zoom NASA's own 3D models. Numbered parts explain what each part is, why it was designed that way and what it helped us learn. A "How it worked" sequence shows the mission step by step. A "1969 vs. today" switch shows that only Eagle's descent stage stayed on the Moon. - Story: each machine answers five questions about its life in a first-person voice. This voice is clearly marked as creative, and every chapter links to its NASA sources. A status card says honestly whether the machine is silent, finished or still in use. - Activities: in the laser activity, students fire a laser pulse at the Moon and use t = 2d/c to find the distance. In the Spirit activity, they compare the rover's solar energy before and after dust covered its panels. - Quiz and log: three questions per machine, with explanations. Progress is saved on the device, and students earn a stamp for each finished machine. - Classroom: a ready 45-minute lesson plan with a worksheet and answer key. Benefits and impact Young people usually hear about new missions and rarely about the machines that came before. Many old mission pages are long and technical. SpaceLegacy turns them into short, visual stories that link each machine's engineering to what it helped us learn. Teachers get a free lesson they can use right away. We have not tested it with students yet, so these are the outcomes we hope for, not measured results. Tools we used HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no build step. Google's model-viewer and the Draco decoder show the 3D models. Python scripts check every content link, file and physics value. The site is static and loads nothing from outside servers at runtime, so it is fast and also works offline. We made the demo video in Blender with NASA 3D models. The site is hosted on Cloudflare. What makes it creative It combines three things in one short journey: exploring real hardware part by part, a story told by the machine itself, and a small hands-on science task. The "1969 vs. today" switch and the laser you can "fire" at the Moon make abstract ideas easy to see. What we considered - Accuracy: 35 sources, all from NASA except the speed of light (NIST). A script checks 176 quoted facts against saved copies of 63 source pages. Creative text is always labelled as creative. - Honesty about status: we separate "mission complete", "lost contact" and "still in use", and show the date we last checked. - Accessibility: full keyboard control, a text list of every 3D part, a "describe this view" panel, labelled controls, reduced-motion support and no audio. If a device cannot show 3D, a NASA image appears instead. - Phones and slow internet: optimized models and images, and a layout tested at phone width. - Rights: NASA images and models are credited and used under NASA's media guidelines. We use no NASA logos, and the site says it is an independent student project, not endorsed by NASA.
